fields.description: Posts tagged with where you are, reactions without counts, and a nudge when someone compatible is nearby.
fields.intro: Sparks is an iOS app concept for keeping up with old friends and meeting new ones, built around where people are. In a team of four at the Product Design Sprint 2025, I made the early directions and designed the final hi-fi screens and the prototype.
fields.summary: Turning a weekend brief about connection into a location-based social app, from map sketches to a wired prototype that opens with a nudge on the lock screen.
fields.overview: Sparks is for people who want to stay close to old friends and make new ones nearby. I worked with Ivy, Derrick and Stella over one weekend. We submitted a wired Figma prototype and a pitch deck, and didn’t place.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we help people build deeper connections with old friends and new ones?
content: That’s a shortened version of the brief at the Product Design Sprint 2025, run by Western Founders Network at Western University. Ivy, Derrick, Stella and I had one weekend to answer it. The organizer’s full question was longer:

content.quote: How might we redesign our digital and social environments to help people build deeper, more meaningful connections despite the challenges of maintaining contact with old friends and creating ones with new acquaintances?

content: The brief asked for a digital product that helps people make meaningful connections, keep in touch with old friends and form new relationships. Our own notes put the problem more bluntly: “more connections than ever but lonelier”, with friendship turned into “just numbers on a screen”.

bullets: **Who:** people trying to stay close to old friends and make new ones.
**Constraint:** one weekend, with a Figma prototype and a PDF deck due Sunday morning.

sections.title: Idea
sections.heading: Borrowed from familiar apps
content: Our brainstorm, titled “Idea: ripples”, borrowed from apps people already use:

bullets: **BeReal’s friends of friends:** meeting people through the ones you know.
**last.fm and Airbuds:** how compatible two people are.
**Bounce,** the app Western used for orientation week: seeing who’s going.

content: Then we wrote a short list of what to go with:

content.caption: Our “Go” list, and where each idea ended up.

content: A note on our Figma canvas also spells out the whole demo, step by step:

content.quote: max is nearby. he wants friends. / prompts yoou to take a photo and write about ur day … / see max’s profile / activities throughout the day + compatability test (x%) / suggest things tp do near

content: The final prototype follows that note closely, from the nudge to the plan. My early screens started somewhere else, though: on a map.

sections.title: Directions
sections.heading: Starting on a map
content: Our brainstorm already had a sketch of a pin at a mall with chat bubbles over it. My lo-fi screens started there, with posts as speech bubbles on the place itself: on a pin, and over a map of Western’s campus next to people’s faces.

content.alt: Two lo-fi iPhone screens: a pink pin for markville mall with the speech bubbles “bruhhhh” and “i just ate chicken!!!!!”, and a map of Western’s campus with two profile pins and the same bubbles
content.caption: Lo-fi: posts as speech bubbles on a pin, and on a map of campus.

content: My other early direction gave it colour: a blue sky with clouds, built around a profile. On maxim’s, the live tab shows where he is on a map, with his latest post and big emoji reactions floating over it. The history tab lays out his posts as a timeline of places and times. On your own profile, a + pin on your map with “Say something...” is where you post.

content.alt: Three iPhones in the blue-sky direction: maxim’s profile with a live map of a mall and floating emoji reactions, his history as a timeline of posts with places and times, and ivy c.’s own profile with a plus pin and Say something...
content.caption: The blue-sky direction: maxim’s live map, his history, and your own profile.

content: In this direction, home was a profile. We moved away from it for two reasons:

bullets: **A profile-first home felt too much like a dating app.**

content: So home became Updates, a feed of posts, and the map moved into it as one of three tabs.

content.alt: Two iPhones: the blue-sky home with maxim’s profile and live map, and the final Updates feed with Location, Map and Friends tabs and ivy c.’s post at Ontario Hall
content.caption: The profile-first home, and the feed that replaced it.

sections.title: Feed
sections.heading: One feed, three lenses
content: Every post in Sparks belongs to a place, and Updates is where they come together. Getting its layout right took a few tries. I designed four versions of the feed:

bullets: Posts grouped under the place they came from, with cards staggered left and right and a black “New Update” button.
A soft gradient behind the posts, and four icons in the nav.
The feed as a sheet over a full-bleed landscape photo.
White again, with Location, Map and Friends at the top and a floating nav with a blue + button.

content.alt: Four versions of the Sparks feed: a white feed grouped under Markville Mall with a black New Update button, the same on a soft green gradient with four nav tabs, the feed as a sheet over a landscape photo, and a white feed with Location, Map and Friends tabs and a blue plus button
content.caption: Four feed versions, in the order they’re numbered in the file.

content: In the final design, the three tabs are three ways to look at what’s been posted:

bullets: **Location** groups posts under the place they were posted, like Ontario Hall.
**Map** shows them as bubbles on a map of campus, around your own blue dot.
**Friends** groups them by person, with a row of posts for each friend.

content.alt: Three iPhones showing the Updates tabs: Location with ivy c.’s posts at Ontario Hall, Map with post bubbles and reactions on a campus map, and Friends with rows of posts from maxim and nomnomburger
content.caption: The three lenses on the final feed.

content: The map never went away. Besides its own tab, it sits at the top of each place page and fills the Live tab on each profile.

sections.title: Posting
sections.heading: Sharing where you are
content: None of this works unless people post. Our demo note named the problem: “ppl don’t have much info about their friends”. Posting changed a few times along the way.
One version asked outright: a “Take a Photo!” sheet to “Update your network”, with a selfie camera, Dismiss and Next, and a step to confirm the photo. It felt pushy.

In the final design, that sheet is gone. A blue + in the nav, on every main screen, opens a small composer for a Zap: a line of text, a photo if you want one, and a placeholder that tells you up front: “Zap. Location will be shared.”

content.alt: The earlier Take a Photo! sheet with a selfie, Dismiss and Next, and the final composer on an iPhone with Zap. Location will be shared., Add photo and Post
content.caption: The “Take a Photo!” sheet, and the composer that replaced it.

content: Add photo opens the camera, and the photo joins your Zap.

content.alt: Three iPhones: the empty composer with Zap. Location will be shared., the camera with a photo of friends in a study room, and the composer with I’m doing PDS at Western and the photo attached
content.caption: Write a Zap, add a photo, post.

content: Two settings decide what others see:

bullets: **Ghost Mode** turns off your live location.
**Post Visibility** picks who sees your posts: Friends, Friends of friends or Public, each with how many people that reaches.

content: Every post also shows who can see it, with a small icon next to its time.

content.alt: Two iPhones showing Privacy settings: Ghost Mode with Disable Live Location, and Post Visibility opened to Friends, 4 people, Friends of friends, 200+ people, and Public, All Users
content.caption: Ghost Mode and Post Visibility, closed and open.

sections.title: Reactions
sections.heading: Who reacted
content: A reaction is the smallest way to start a conversation. We borrowed the idea from Strava’s kudos: something that “breaks the ice” and is “more casual than replying to IG stories”. A friend’s post carries a row of them, 🍴, 😋, 😭 and 💀, with a button to add your own and “Send a reply” underneath.

What a post never shows is a count. Open one, and each reaction appears as a chip with the name of the person who left it. No post or profile in the prototype counts reactions, friends or followers. That came straight from our list: “No numbers!!”

content.alt: Two iPhones: the Friends tab with maxim’s post i just ate chicken!!, and the post opened, with each reaction shown as a chip with a name, a React! button and a reply bar
content.caption: Tap a post to see who reacted, by name.

content: The card changed along the way. In the feed versions, Reply and the reactions sat in one row under the post. In the final card, the reactions moved inside it, “Send a reply” sits below, and the time and who can see the post sit in the corner.

gallery.label: Final

sections.title: Meeting
sections.heading: From nearby to a plan
content: Meeting someone new is the other half of the brief, and in Sparks it starts on your lock screen: “👀 Psst... maxim is nearby!” and “✨ You and maxim have a high compatibility!”

That nudge is where our demo begins. It opens Sparks straight into the composer, and after you post, you land on maxim’s profile: where he is right now, “92% compatible with Max” and a big “Find things to do!” button.

content.alt: Three iPhones: the lock screen with the notification Psst... maxim is nearby!, maxim’s profile with a live map, 92% compatible with Max and Find things to do!, and Things to do with nearby suggestions
content.caption: The nudge, maxim’s profile and Things to do. In the demo, you post a Zap in between.

content: Things to do lists places nearby, each with how far away it is and why it’s suggested for the two of you. Our demo note already had that idea, in a much wilder form:

content.quote: ur both adventorouous! maybe u should go skinny dipping in thames..

content: In the prototype, it became real places nearby: bouldering at the Junction Climbing Centre, “Suggested because: you are both active”, or a bagelwich at The Spoke for two coffee lovers.

content.alt: Two Things to do cards: Junction Climbing Centre, 3km, Go bouldering at the Junction for only $35!, suggested because you are both active, and The Spoke, 0.5km, Go grab a bagelwich or coffee at the spoke!, suggested because you are both coffee lovers
content.caption: Every suggestion says why.

content: The prototype doesn’t show how the compatibility score is worked out. Our note ties matches to your preferences, “change ur preferences to see ur matches”, and Settings has a Friend Preferences page with an age range, distance, hobbies and what you’re looking for, from a Gym Bro to a Study Buddy.

sections.title: Old friends
sections.heading: Keeping in touch
content: Not every friend is nearby. The brief also asked about keeping in touch with old friends, and in Sparks that happens in Messages: your friends as a cloud of faces, with the latest message peeking out beside one of them.

Tap a face, and the chat opens. In the demo chat, one friend has just got back to Toronto and asks how the prep for the competition is going. The answer: “i’ll update you through the day so it feels like you’re doing it with us”.

content.alt: Two iPhones: Messages with friends as round photos and a preview bubble, and a chat with emily with a photo, blue message bubbles and a reply about PDS
content.caption: Messages as faces, then a chat.

content: Settings also has a Best Friends list. Add someone to it, and you get more notifications from their activity.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: Results
content: We submitted the wired prototype and our pitch deck by the Sunday morning deadline. Sparks didn’t place. The final screens on this page are exactly what we submitted, with no polish after.
It’s a concept from one weekend. The people, places, scores and suggestions in the screens are sample data.

Sparks answered a weekend brief about connection with an app built around where people are. Posts carry a place, reactions show names instead of counts, and a nudge on the lock screen leads to someone compatible nearby and a list of things to do together.
In a team with Ivy, Derrick and Stella, I made the early map and blue-sky directions, then designed the final screens and the wired prototype.
